cf.title: Showing "Table Block Fetches" in EXPLAIN ANALYZE for index-only scans

input.subject: Showing "Table Block Fetches" in EXPLAIN ANALYZE for index-only scans

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection disputes counting table blocks, and both replies support it. The two surviving objections, demand-1 and standards-compat-1, are fixable and concern the same point: version 1 removes the "Heap Fetches" line, which both reviewers want kept and which tools parse by key name. The author offered in message #1 to report both counts, so a next version can settle this.

brief.title: Show table block fetches instead of heap fetches for index-only scans
brief.problem: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows "Heap Fetches" for index-only scans, which counts tuples whose visibility had to be checked in the table. The author says this is only a rough proxy for the real cost to users of heap pages not being all-visible in the visibility map.
brief.proposed_design: The patch replaces "Heap Fetches" with "Table Block Fetches", the number of times the scan switched to a different table block, which is one ReadBuffer call per fetch. The counter lives in heapam, made easier by commit ddce1da5. Version 1 drops the tuple count, but the author offers to report both.
user_visible_surface: EXPLAIN ANALYZE output for Index Only Scan nodes: "Heap Fetches" line removed, "Table Block Fetches" line added.
IndexScanInstrumentation-related struct in instrument_node.h changes, visible to extensions that read executor instrumentation.
author_claims: Block fetches show the exact physical cost of pages not being all-visible, not a rough proxy.
The count is table AM agnostic, at least in theory.
Repeated rescans that touch only the same heap page report a single block fetch.
The current tuple-based counter may exist mainly because a block count was awkward to do in nodeIndexonlyscan.c before ddce1da5.
brief.thread_state: Sami Imseih and Greg Burd support counting blocks but both want a tuple count kept, with Sami suggesting "Table Tuple Fetches" and exposure in pg_stat_*_indexes. Greg also asks whether the same fields could later appear on plain Index Scan nodes; the author has not replied.
unclear: The patch does not say how tools and scripts that parse "Heap Fetches" from EXPLAIN text, JSON or XML output should cope with the removed key.
The material does not say whether the change to the instrumentation struct breaks extensions such as pg_stat_statements or auto_explain consumers.
The material does not say how parallel index-only scans add up block fetches across workers.
The material does not say why nodeIndexscan.c and nodeBitmapIndexscan.c are touched, or whether their output changes.
search_queries: explain index only scan visibility map

objections.title: No one in the thread asks to remove the Heap Fetches line
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA watches "Heap Fetches" in auto_explain logs or EXPLAIN JSON to tell when VACUUM is falling behind on an index-only scan. After upgrading, the key is gone and their check finds nothing. The scan that used to show many fetched tuples on a few pages now shows a small block count, so the alert stays quiet.
objections.argument: Both replies want a block count, and both also want the tuple count kept (messages #2 and #3). Message #3 gives a case where only the two counters together show stale entries. Removing the line costs every existing reader of EXPLAIN output, while the gain is a shorter plan. The author offers to report both in message #1, but v1 still removes the line.
objections.author_must_show: Which users or workloads gain from removing the tuple count, as opposed to adding a block count next to it?

critic.reasoning: Both replies ask to keep the tuple count, and message #3 gives a case that needs both counters. The author's offer depends on consensus and version 1 still drops the count, so the material does not yet answer this.

objections.title: Removing the "Heap Fetches" key breaks existing EXPLAIN consumers
objections.failure_scenario: A monitoring tool or auto_explain log parser reads "Heap Fetches" from FORMAT JSON output to flag tables whose visibility map needs vacuum. After upgrade the key is absent, so the check finds nothing and reports every index-only scan as clean. The DBA finds out only when someone notices the alert stopped firing.
objections.argument: "Heap Fetches" has long been the standard signal that index-only scans are hitting the heap, and the JSON, XML and YAML formats exist so that tools can depend on key names. Version 1 drops the key, and Sami's suggested "Table Tuple Fetches" in message #2 would rename it, which still breaks those parsers. Messages #2 and #3 ask to keep a tuple count, but neither says it should keep its current name. A committer would likely prefer adding the new line and keeping "Heap Fetches" unchanged unless a rename is argued separately.
objections.author_must_show: Why should the tuple counter not stay under its existing "Heap Fetches" key, with "Table Block Fetches" added beside it?

critic.reasoning: Version 1 removes the "Heap Fetches" key, and the proposal does not say how tools that parse the structured formats should cope. The author's offer to report both counts does not settle whether the existing key name stays.

refuted.title: New "Table Block" wording departs from existing "Heap Blocks" output
refuted.failure_scenario: A user reads a plan containing both a Bitmap Heap Scan with "Heap Blocks: exact=N" and an Index Only Scan with "Table Block Fetches: M". The two names suggest two different kinds of block, so the user cannot easily compare table page access between the two nodes.
refuted.argument: EXPLAIN already reports table page counts as "Heap Blocks" on bitmap heap scans. Message #1 gives table AM neutrality as the reason to avoid "heap", which is a fair aim. The proposal applies the new term to one node only and leaves the existing heap-named fields as they are. A departure from existing naming needs a plan for the other fields, or a reason why one node should differ.
refuted.author_must_show: Is "Table" meant to become the EXPLAIN term for all table-page counters, and if so, what happens to "Heap Blocks"?

critic.reasoning: "Heap Blocks" on a Bitmap Heap Scan counts exact and lossy bitmap pages, a different quantity, so the scenario of a failed comparison is not a failure. Message #1 gives table AM neutrality as the reason and leaves the name open.

refuted.title: Removing the "Heap Fetches" key breaks tools that parse EXPLAIN output
refuted.failure_scenario: A monitoring tool reads the "Heap Fetches" key from auto_explain JSON to flag tables that need VACUUM. After upgrade the key is gone, so the tool reports nothing or zero. Nobody notices until an index-only scan regression goes undetected in production.
refuted.argument: "Heap Fetches" has been in text, JSON, XML and YAML EXPLAIN output for many releases, and external plan visualizers and auto_explain pipelines parse it. V1 removes it without a transition, and the patch prose does not mention format consumers. Messages #2 and #3 both ask to keep a tuple count, and message #1 offers to do so, but the author has not yet chosen. Keeping the old key unchanged costs little, while renaming or dropping it puts the cost on every downstream tool.
refuted.author_must_show: Will the next version keep the existing "Heap Fetches" key with its current meaning beside the new counter, and if not, why is the break worth it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which states the same parser break and asks the sharper question about keeping the existing key name.

refuted.title: Table AMs that do not maintain the new counter silently report zero
refuted.failure_scenario: An out-of-core table AM uses the slot-based index scan interface but does not update the block counter. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows "Table Block Fetches: 0" on its index-only scans. A user reads that as "all pages visible" and stops investigating a slow query.
refuted.argument: After ddce1da5 the counter lives in heapam (message #1), so every table AM must maintain it, and nothing fails when an AM does not. Zero is also the value that means "no extra cost", so a missing count looks like a good result. Message #3 already proposes filling the same fields from another AM and on plain Index Scan nodes, so the struct in instrument_node.h is becoming an AM-facing API. The proposal does not define what an AM must count or how EXPLAIN shows an AM that does not report.
refuted.author_must_show: What does the table AM API require of each AM for this counter, and how does EXPLAIN distinguish "zero fetches" from "not reported"?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 says commit ddce1da5 already made the table AM responsible for the "Heap Fetches" counter. An AM that does not count already shows zero today, so the patch does not create this gap.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch changes the index scan instrumentation struct in instrument_node.h, which table AMs fill and extensions can read.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Removing the "Heap Fetches" key from text, JSON, XML and YAML output puts a change on every tool that parses it.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch changes counter maintenance in heapam_indexscan.c, which runs during index-only scans; no cost concern survived review.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection demand-1: No one in the thread asks to remove the Heap Fetches line

questions: Will the next version keep the tuple count under the existing "Heap Fetches" key and add "Table Block Fetches" beside it, and if not, why?
Which users or workloads gain from removing the tuple count, as opposed to adding the block count next to it?
How does a parallel index-only scan add up table block fetches across workers, given that two workers can fetch the same block?
Why does the patch touch nodeIndexscan.c and nodeBitmapIndexscan.c, and does EXPLAIN output for those nodes change?
Are the same instrumentation fields meant to be shown later on plain Index Scan nodes, filled by the table AM, as message #3 asks?

committability.owner_note: The author states in message #1 that he committed ddce1da5, the table AM index scan interface this patch builds on.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a permanent change to EXPLAIN ANALYZE key names that external tools parse, and for the meaning of an instrumentation counter that each table AM must maintain.
committability.author_follow_up: The author offers in message #1 to produce a revision that reports both counts; he has not yet replied to messages #2 and #3.

priority.reason: The patch is about 25 KiB, mostly EXPLAIN code, docs and expected test output, and two reviewers support the block count. The open point is whether "Heap Fetches" stays, which a second version can settle.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check how the block counter behaves across rescans and parallel workers. It also could not check what the changes in nodeIndexscan.c and nodeBitmapIndexscan.c do.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
Reverted commit(s): Fix index-only scan plans when not all index columns can be returned.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 4ace45677 failed to fix the problem fully, because the
same issue of attempting to fetch a non-returnable index column
can occur when rechecking the indexqual after using a lossy index
operator.  Moreover, it broke EXPLAIN for such indexquals (which
indicates a gap in our test cases :-().

Revert the code changes of 4ace45677 in favor of adding a new field
to struct IndexOnlyScan, containing a version of the indexqual that
can be executed against the index-returned tuple without using any
non-returnable columns.  (The restrictions imposed by check_index_only
guarantee this is possible, although we may have to recompute indexed
expressions.)  Support construction of that during setrefs.c
processing by marking IndexOnlyScan.indextlist entries as resjunk
if they can't be returned, rather than removing them entirely.
(We could alternatively require setrefs.c to look up the IndexOptInfo
again, but abusing resjunk this way seems like a reasonably safe way
to avoid needing to do that.)

This solution isn't great from an API-stability standpoint: if there
are any extensions out there that build IndexOnlyScan structs directly,
they'll be broken in the next minor releases.  However, only a very
invasive extension would be likely to do such a thing.  There's no
change in the Path representation, so typical planner extensions
shouldn't have a problem.

As before, back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.title: Index Only Scan for index expressions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch extends the planner so that index-only scans can be used when a query's target list or restriction clauses contain expressions that exactly match index expression columns, not only plain attribute columns. Matching requires the expression tree (or a subtree) to be identical to the index expression; no normalization of commutative or associative operators is attempted.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Testing of the sixth patch version by Vladimir Sitnikov found an error ("variable not found in subplan target list") when queries access non-indexed columns alongside an expression index. Robert Haas marked the entry Returned with Feedback because these bugs precluded committing it before the CommitFest ended, while inviting resubmission and saying the effort was good.

precedents_retrieved.key_quote:

preclude committing it, so I'm marking it "Returned with Feedback" for

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix buffer pinning logic/visibility bugs in [SP-]Gist Index-Only Scans
precedents_retrieved.authors: Peter Geoghegan (pgeoghegan), Michail Nikolaev (nkey), Matthias van de Meent (mmeent), Mihail Nikalayeu (mihailnikalayeu)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a race in GiST and SP-GiST index-only scans, where concurrent VACUUM can remove a TID and set the visibility map bit before the scan checks it, so a dead tuple is returned. Later versions drop the idea of holding pins on index pages: they add a table AM API (table_index_vischeck_tuples) so the index AM checks the visibility map while it still holds the page pin, and they also change nbtree to use it.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last visible message (v14, December 2025) only fixes a CFBot failure, and the entry was withdrawn about six months later with no visible objection or explanation. The author had moved a backpatchable version of the fix to a separate thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use tuple-level SIREAD locks for index-only scans
precedents_retrieved.summary: Index-only scans that skip the heap would take tuple-level SIREAD locks instead of locking the whole heap page, with a fix to the outdated comment in nodeIndexonlyscan.c. A later experimental patch also skipped the btree page lock when the scan uses equality quals on all key columns of a unique index.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stopped applying after a collision in the test files, and Daniel Gustafsson asked for a rebased version. No new version appears in the visible messages, so the entry was returned with feedback. Earlier, David Rowley found that deferrable unique constraints broke the btree lock skip, and Thomas Munro fixed that case in v4. Thomas Munro was still unsure the fix covered every case.

precedents_retrieved.title: Index Only Scan support for cube
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a GiST fetch function for the cube extension so that queries on cube columns can use Index Only Scans. It reuses g_cube_decompress() as the fetch function, since both only need to detoast the key.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it as obsolete after commit d3a4f89 (Allow no-op GiST support functions to be omitted). He said he would work on a broader patch for contrib modules to support GiST Index Only Scans and remove no-op support functions.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add parallel columns for seq scan and index scan on pg_stat_all_tables and _indexes
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds parallel_seq_scan, last_parallel_seq_scan, parallel_idx_scan and last_parallel_idx_scan columns to pg_stat_all_tables, and parallel_idx_scan and last_parallel_idx_scan to pg_stat_all_indexes. The goal is to help administrators judge how parallel workers are used and tune parallelism settings.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers doubted that per-table and per-index counts of parallel scans help with tuning, since parallel plans with Gather nodes are usually analyzed per statement. Michael Paquier added that the metrics committed in e7a9496de906 and 5d4298e75f25 may already cover the need. Robert Haas found no clear use case for these counters. The author agreed that the committed metrics were good enough for now.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think the question to which we don't have a clear answer is: for what purpose would you want to be able to distinguish parallel and non-parallel scans on a per-table basis?

precedents_retrieved.title: EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW
precedents_retrieved.summary: Allow EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE on REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, showing the plan of the view's defining SELECT (plain EXPLAIN without refreshing, EXPLAIN ANALYZE performing the refresh), analogous to existing EXPLAIN support for CREATE TABLE AS / CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW. A companion patch refactored ExecRefreshMatView into smaller functions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that supporting EXPLAIN would bind REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW to having an explainable SQL plan, constraining future implementations such as incremental view maintenance, while offering little beyond explaining the view's query directly; the author agreed to withdraw the feature. The leftover refactoring patch was also not taken, because John Naylor judged it would conflict with the refactoring in the pending incremental view maintenance patch without helping it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The problem with it is that it
binds us to the assumption that REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW has an
explainable plan.

precedents_retrieved.title: Sampling-based timing for EXPLAIN ANALYZE
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a TIMING SAMPLING mode to EXPLAIN ANALYZE that records a timestamp from a recurring timer (up to 1000 Hz) instead of reading the clock in InstrStartNode/InstrStopNode. Each node's sampled time is scaled to total wall clock time to keep overhead close to TIMING OFF.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread went stale after January and the patch stopped building on the CFBot, so Daniel Gustafsson returned it with feedback. Earlier review asked whether sampling still pays off once the RDTSC patch lands. It also noted that fast nodes get zero sampled time, and suggested hybrid designs that time early or rarely called nodes exactly; the author did not post a new version.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This thread has been stale since January with no movement at all during the
March CF, and according to the CFBot it stopped building at all ~ 14 weeks ago.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support SK_SEARCHNULL / SK_SEARCHNOTNULL for heap-only scans
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes heap scans honor SK_SEARCHNULL and SK_SEARCHNOTNULL scan keys in HeapKeyTest(), which skey.h documents as supported only for index scans. The goal was convenience for extensions that scan tables directly without SPI; a later follow-up by Jacob Champion added planner pushdown of IS [NOT] NULL quals into Seq Scan as scan keys.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas saw no benefit in heapam support alone and asked that nodeSeqScan.c use it, with performance results, and that the table AM API get an 'amsearchnulls' field. The author wanted to defer the executor part to a later patch, so Heikki marked the entry Returned with Feedback. The later executor and planner patches got no visible review before the entry closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Ok, I don't think this patch on its own is a good idea, without the
other parts, so I'll mark this as Returned with Feedback in the commitfest.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found for this idea. [P19] adds an EXPLAIN counter for bitmap heap scans, a different node and a different counter, and it records no reason, so nothing from it applies here. The thread does not point to any earlier discussion of block-level fetch counts for index-only scans.
The idea of counting table blocks is not disputed from this angle. The objections concern only the output contract and naming.

The patch changes only EXPLAIN ANALYZE output and an in-memory instrumentation struct. It writes nothing to disk, WAL, catalogs or the wire protocol, so there is nothing for pg_upgrade, standbys or subscribers to handle. The instrument_node.h change goes into master only, and extensions already rebuild for each major version. Parallel workers share that struct within one server binary. Exposing the counts in pg_stat_*_indexes, as message #2 suggests, would add pgstat state, but that is not part of this patch.

The proposal changes which counter EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows for index-only scans. The block count reaches the same user, through the same command, who can already run the query and see its buffer counts, so it adds no new privilege, exposure or denial-of-service path. The suggested pg_stat_*_indexes exposure is not part of v1.
Two fixable objections only. The per-block counter adds no meaningful hot-path cost, and a committer who knows the area wrote the patch.

No existing feature gives per-node table block fetches for an index-only scan. EXPLAIN (BUFFERS) mixes index, visibility map and heap buffers in one number, and pg_statio_user_tables heap_blks_hit/read are per table and cumulative, so neither can isolate this scan node. No extension or external tool that does this is known with certainty, and the counter needs table AM internals, so it cannot easily live outside core. [P19] is about bitmap heap scans, has no recorded reason, and does not apply.
The block count itself has support from two independent reviewers and a concrete cost case in message #2. The only demand gap is the removal of the existing tuple count.
